lessons.student_outcome: Authorise a practice transfer on Devnet and verify execution separately from commitment.
prereqs: A practice wallet on Solana Devnet; no prior Solana required.
objectives: Separate submission, execution result, and commitment.
Reject a wallet request that does not match intention.
Verify a transfer on the intended network before claiming success.

learning_loop.objective: Predict fee and balance changes — then verify execution separately from commitment.
learning_loop.predict_question: You approve a Devnet transfer of 0.01 SOL from A to B. What must be true before you treat it as a successful practical transfer?

predict_options.label: A transaction signature appears in the wallet UI
It is observed on Devnet, execution succeeded, and it reached the required commitment
The fee was zero, so commitment does not matter

learning_loop.predict_why: A signature identifier is not proof of successful execution or of the required commitment. Check network, execution result, and commitment as separate dimensions.
learning_loop.act: Use the lesson’s practice transfer or observation route. Review the wallet request against your prediction before approving. Prefer Devnet. Do not use mainnet funds.
learning_loop.explain_question: Why can a transaction be confirmed on the network and still have failed execution while charging a fee?
learning_loop.transfer: Without re-reading the full lesson: a transaction id is visible. What three checks do you make before claiming success?

prereqs: Lesson 001 — Authorise and verify a transaction (or equivalent).
objectives: Identify an account’s owner program vs authorities in its data.
Predict who must sign an update.
Explain why the wrong signer fails.

learning_loop.objective: Separate program ownership from authority — then predict who must sign an update.
learning_loop.predict_question: A profile account’s owner program is ProfileProgram. The profile data names Alice as authority. Who must sign a name update that ProfileProgram will accept?

predict_options.label: Anyone who can deploy ProfileProgram
Alice (the authority named in the account data), per the program’s rules
Any wallet that can see the account address

learning_loop.predict_why: The owner program enforces the update rules. Authority lives in the account’s data (or related accounts), not in “I can see the address.” The wrong signer fails even if the owner program is correct.
learning_loop.act: Inspect the Lesson 002 cases: authorised vs unauthorised update. Record owner program, data length, and who is named as authority before claiming control.
learning_loop.explain_question: Why can “this is my wallet” and “this account’s owner is a program” both be true without contradiction?
learning_loop.transfer: Given only an address, list three things you will not infer about control or real-world identity.

assessment_misconceptions.title: Authority vs ownership
assessment_misconceptions.misconception: Putting my address in the authority field automatically prevents other people from changing the data.

learning_loop.objective: Trace an instruction’s program, accounts, and data — then predict the state change.
learning_loop.predict_question: You prepare an “Update profile” instruction. Which three components must you identify before predicting the account change?

learning_loop.objective: Predict all-or-nothing application state when a later instruction fails.
learning_loop.predict_question: A transaction has two instructions: (1) update profile name, (2) record a log that depends on the new name. Instruction 2 fails during execution. What happens to the profile name on-chain?

predict_options.label: The name update from instruction 1 remains; only instruction 2 reverts
Neither instruction’s application-state change remains — the transaction rolls back
Both changes remain because a fee was charged

learning_loop.predict_why: Solana transactions are atomic for program state changes: if a later instruction fails, earlier instruction effects in that transaction do not persist. A fee may still be charged.
learning_loop.act: Walk the Lesson 004 investigator cases. List instructions in order, then predict state when a later step fails.
learning_loop.explain_question: How can a failed multi-instruction transaction leave profile state unchanged while still charging a fee?
learning_loop.transfer: Distinguish one multi-instruction transaction from two separate transactions in one sentence.

learning_loop.objective: Locate the failure stage — then choose a recovery that avoids blind resubmit.
learning_loop.predict_question: The wallet UI shows a signature, then the app times out. You never saw a confirmed execution result. What is the safest next move?

predict_options.label: Immediately approve the same transfer again
Reconcile the existing attempt (network, signature, execution) before any replacement
Treat “not observed” as proof it never happened and move on

learning_loop.predict_why: Unresolved observation is not proof of non-execution. Blind resubmit can double-apply a business action. Reconcile first.
learning_loop.act: Use Lesson 005 scenarios: wallet rejection, simulation failure, execution failure, and timeout. Classify each before recovering.
learning_loop.explain_question: Why must you separate “not observed” from “did not happen”?
learning_loop.transfer: Name four failure stages and one recovery rule that applies to all of them.

assessment_misconceptions.title: UI error vs on-chain execution
assessment_misconceptions.misconception: The page displayed an error, so the transaction must have executed and failed.

assessment_misconceptions.title: Timeout as proof of non-execution
assessment_misconceptions.misconception: Treating a timeout or one null status as proof that the operation never happened.

learning_loop.objective: Keep observed account data separate from drafts and pending updates.
learning_loop.predict_question: Your update transaction succeeded on Devnet, but the UI still shows the old name. What should you do first?

predict_options.label: Press Save again immediately with the same draft
Re-read the account with an appropriate commitment/context and reconcile before editing again
Assume the transaction failed because the UI did not update

learning_loop.predict_why: UI staleness is not proof of failed execution. Reconcile observed account data against the attempt before repeating a write.
learning_loop.act: In Lesson 006, label observed vs draft vs pending vs outcome on a profile update. Preserve drafts when a conflict is detected.
learning_loop.explain_question: Why should a failed refresh not be recorded as proof that an update did not execute?

assessment_misconceptions.title: Input vs account state
assessment_misconceptions.misconception: The input contains the new name, so the profile is updated.

learning_loop.objective: Explain expected-revision checks — and why silently refreshing then resubmitting is unsafe.
learning_loop.predict_question: Tab A and Tab B both read revision 12. Tab A’s update lands first (revision becomes 13). Tab B still submits expected_revision=12. What should a correctly guarded program do?

predict_options.label: Accept Tab B and overwrite Tab A’s change
Reject Tab B because expected_revision does not match current state
Silently bump expected_revision to 13 and apply Tab B without review

learning_loop.predict_why: Expected-revision / concurrency checks reject stale writes. Silently refreshing the revision and resubmitting can overwrite intervening work the user never reviewed.
learning_loop.act: Run Lesson 007’s competing-edit cases. Record starting revision, each tab’s expected revision, and which request the program accepts.
learning_loop.explain_question: Why must authorisation checks stay separate from the expected-revision check?
learning_loop.transfer: After a stale-write rejection, what three steps replace “silently refresh and resubmit”?
